finding: NOT CHECKED: this file holds labor times only, so it can neither confirm nor contradict the live range of $180-$925. The run's shared web-search limit was reached before any parts price or any benchmark could be loaded, so every parts figure is null, there are no benchmarks and no totals can be built. Nothing here should be used to change the live range. What was verified is the labor side, from manufacturer bulletins. One easy-to-reach mount on a small car or crossover is a short job at warranty pace: 0.7 hr for the side mount on a 2012-15 Honda Civic Si, 0.6 hr for the No.3 mount on a Mazda3 or CX-5 2.0L, 0.5 hr for the rear mount on a Jeep Compass. At $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks) that is about $60-$112 of labor before the part. Engine mounts on body-on-frame trucks and SUVs take much longer: GM allows 3.1-3.2 hr to replace both on a 2014-2018 Silverado/Sierra and 3.8 hr on the SUVs, FCA allows 3.9 hr for both on a 2021-2022 Jeep Grand Cherokee, but only 1.4 hr for both on a Ram 2500 6.4L; 3.2 hr is about $384-$512 of labor. A transmission mount on a 2019-2020 Silverado is 0.5 hr. How solid the labor times are: economy is for the example vehicle (the Si model). Midsize is the right model but an engine not sold in the United States. Truck and luxury are for the example vehicles but for BOTH mounts; no manufacturer states a time for one side, so the low end is null and the high end is a ceiling at warranty pace, not what a shop would bill for one mount. All are warranty times, the low end of what shops bill. No stated time was found for an active or electronically controlled mount on a mainstream car (Honda and Acura V6 models use them); the only active-mount figure found is Porsche's 685-761 time units for both mounts on a 2020 911, which was not converted to hours. Nissan (2019 Altima, 2021-2024 Rogue left mount) and GM (2021 Buick Envision) bulletins name the operation but refer to their flat-rate manuals without printing a time. Still needed before this job can be judged: for each class an OEM list price and an aftermarket price for the named mount, and at least three benchmarks.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or inspection fee (finding which mount has failed), new one-time-use mount bolts and nuts (the Honda bulletin calls for four new bolts and a nut with one mount), and a second or third mount, since they tend to wear together and some makers replace them only in pairs. Active, hydraulic (fluid-filled) and electronically controlled mounts cost far more than plain rubber ones and may need a separate actuator or vacuum line. On some vehicles the job needs an engine support, removal of the splash shields or exhaust parts, or a wheel alignment if the subframe is loosened. Also shop supplies and sales tax.
